newsitem.title: POLAND: FEATURE - Polish insurers far from ready for foreign rivals.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Polish insurers far from ready for foreign rivals.

text.p: Two years before the doors to Poland's promising insurance market swing fully open, domestic insurers still have a long way to go before they are fit to face foreign competition.

Analysts say the Polish market offers outstanding growth potential but small domestic firms, still dwarfed by the two former communist-era state monopolists, are not ready to exploit the market's opportunites as they lack sufficient capital and expertise.

Poland, with its 38 million people and annual economic growth of more than five percent, is still a largely unexploited market for insurers with levels of saturation well below those of developed countries.
"There are 13 million employed in Poland and only one million individually insured," said Marian Miziolek, the president of Commercial Union Plc's Polish subsidiary.
He said life insurance in particular was still a fairly new concept for Poles.

Jan Monkiewicz, president of Poland's largest insurer, the state-owned Powszechny Zaklad Ubezpieczen SA (PZU), said an estimated 20 percent growth in premium revenue last year should continue for the next five to seven years.
"There is a growth in premiums of 20 percent in real terms and this...is obviously just a start," Monkiewicz said.

In the first three quarters of 1996, Polish insurers collected a total of 6.1 billion zlotys ($2.13 billion) in gross premiums against 5.6 billion zloty premium revenue in the whole of 1995 a report by the Central Statistical Office (GUS) showed.
REALISING FULL POTENTIAL TO TAKE TIME

But insurers say realising the full potential of the Polish market requires time and perseverance as growth is hampered by the still relatively low incomes of Poles and their reluctance to spend much to insure against various risks.
The potentially high-growth life insurance segment is limited by a lack of relevant regulations on the creation of private pension funds and by unfavourable tax treatment.

Poland's long-discussed social security reform, aimed at overhauling the heavily-subsidised state pension scheme, has yet to materialise and contributions to optional pension plans offered by life insurers are not tax deductible.
Anatol Adamski, head of the finance ministry's insurance department, said the government would have to offer incentives to spur the sector's growth.
"If we are serious about growth in life insurance, there will have to be some impulses in the longer term, but there are no defined plans yet," Adamski told Reuters.
FOREIGNERS DO BETTER THAN POLISH FIRMS

Only after 1999 will foreign insurers gain unlimited access to the Polish market. Until then, in order to operate they must invest in Polish firms, set up joint ventures or fully-owned subsidiaries and apply for a finance ministry licence.
But those international insurers who have decided to enter the Polish market early are already reporting faster growth than domestic firms and are expanding market share.

According to last month's Nowa Europa daily insurance survey, Commercial Union boosted its share of the life market to 10.7 percent at the end of the third quarter of 1996, up from 6.5 percent in 1995.
Amplico Life, a joint-venture of Polish state-owned bank Pekao SA and the U.S. American Insurance Group (AIG) controls 7.1 percent of the market, against 4.6 percent last year.
Adamski said he expected the next two years to bring the entry of several more leading foreign insurers eager to establish a presence before their rivals.
LOW CAPITAL LIMITS POLISH PLAYERS' GROWTH

Analysts said most of Poland's 40 insurance companies were much too small to compete with PZU and Warta, the country's sole insurers before the fall of communism, which remain dominant despite a slight fall in market share and unspectacular earnings.
Even market leader PZU, which has about 65 percent of the non-life insurance market and, through its life subsidiary, about 78 percent of the life sector, has inadequate capital.
"PZU's capital of 90 million zlotys is ridiculously low," Monkiewicz said.
PZU wants to boost its shareholder equity by a private placement to financial institutions worth 250-750 million zlotys in the first quarter of this year.

Analysts and regulators have said inadequate capital was one of the main reasons for the failures of four small insurers last year, which made many clients leave private insurers and return to the state-owned PZU.

The finance ministry's Adamski said another reason for Polish insurers' problems was their focus on motor insurance, which guaranteed fast premiums growth but generated losses because of the soaring cost of damage.

An analyst at Bank Handlowy SA, Robert Sobieraj, said low capital and insufficient expertise would make it hard even for the largest Polish insurers to compete with foreign giants unless they joined forces with other financial institutions.
RESCUE IN CONSOLIDATION
Sobieraj said Warta, which last month announced plans to set up a financial group with four Polish banks and is seeking a strategic investor, set a good example for other insurers.
"They (insurers) have to do something to avoid giving in to foreign competition and creating banking-insurance groups seems to be the right way to go," Sobieraj said.
But Adamski was sceptical over whether smaller firms would follow Warta's example.
"I somehow can't believe in the...consolidation of smaller firms, as they seem too eager to run the business themselves," he said. ($1=2.8645 Zloty)
